s1.title: Should I really get a divorce? What your hesitation already tells you
s1.p1: You didn't open this page by accident. When someone types "should I get a divorce" into Google, it's not out of idle curiosity. It's because something, somewhere, isn't working anymore, and the question is starting to take up a space you can no longer ignore.
s1.p2: Hesitation, in itself, is already information. It says you don't want to decide in haste. That you take your relationship, and your life, seriously. That matters.
s1.p3: But it can also keep you in an uncomfortable situation indefinitely, if it's never addressed honestly.

s2.title: When should you really consider divorce?
s2.intro: There's no checklist that automatically triggers a separation. But certain signs, when they accumulate and persist, deserve to be taken seriously.
s2.h3_1: When communication has been broken for a long time
s2.h3_1_p1: Not just "we argue", every couple does that. But when you no longer really talk to each other, when important topics have become off-limits, when you feel lonelier together than you do alone.
s2.h3_2: When your repair attempts haven't changed anything
s2.h3_2_p1: Couples therapy, big conversations, promises to change... if all of that has been tried, multiple times, without lasting results, it's not necessarily a lack of effort. It may be a sign that the problem is beyond what you can solve together.
s2.h3_3_p1: Chronic anxiety, sleep disorders, social isolation, feeling like you no longer recognize yourself, your body and mind eventually speak when you don't listen. If your relationship is wearing you down physically and mentally, that's a signal you have no right to minimize.
s2.h3_4: When there is violence, in any form
s2.h3_4_p1: Physical, verbal, psychological. Violence in a relationship doesn't resolve itself, and it doesn't "deserve" a second, or tenth, chance. If you're in this situation, your safety is the priority. Our toxic relationship test can also help you assess this dimension.
s2.tip: You don't need a "good enough reason" to consider divorce. No longer being happy, no longer feeling in your place, no longer wanting to build with this person, that's enough. You don't have to justify your well-being.

s3.title: The real reasons people stay when they should leave
s3.intro: Some reasons to stay in a relationship are solid. Love, the desire to build something, the belief that the relationship can evolve. But other reasons are traps, comfortable, understandable, but traps nonetheless.
s3.h3_1: Fear of hurting the other person
s3.h3_1_p1: Staying out of guilt means delaying suffering while creating more, for you, and ultimately for them too.
s3.h3_2_p1: This is the most common reason, and the most complex. Children need stability, that's true. But they also need parents who are doing well. A home with constant tension, heavy atmosphere, adults coexisting without speaking, that's not stability. It's a facade.
s3.h3_3_p1: Starting over is scary. Especially when you've built a shared life, a social circle, a routine. But staying with someone just to not be alone is choosing a disguised form of loneliness.
s3.h3_4_p1: Legitimate. Divorce has a cost, and when you share property, debt, or a standard of living, financial aspects weigh heavily. But it's a practical obstacle to manage, not a reason to spend your life in a relationship that no longer suits you.
s3.h3_5_p1: Hope is a beautiful thing. It becomes a problem when it's been used to justify inaction for years, waiting for a change that never comes.
s3.tip: If you're staying mainly out of fear, of loneliness, of what others think, of the process, of the future, that's an honest starting point. But fear is not a reliable compass for making a decision this important.

s4.title: How to be sure you're making the right decision?
s4.intro: The truth is, you can never be 100% certain. Divorce, like marriage, is a leap, you don't know exactly what's on the other side. But you can make this decision in the most informed way possible.
s4.h3_1: Take an honest assessment, not just an emotional one
s4.h3_1_p1: In moments of crisis, everything seems final. In good moments, we tend to minimize everything. This test is one tool among others, but keeping a journal for a few weeks, noting how you feel daily, can give a more realistic picture than your emotions at a single moment.
s4.h3_2_p1: Not necessarily to "save" your relationship, but to take stock of yourself. A good therapist won't tell you what to do. They'll help you hear what you truly think, beneath the layers of guilt, fear, and exhaustion.
s4.h3_3: Talk to a lawyer, even just to understand
s4.h3_3_p1: Many people put this off because they're afraid it will "make things real." But getting information doesn't commit you to anything. Understanding your rights, the options available to you, the practical implications, that's information, not a commitment.
s4.h3_4: Give yourself time... but not indefinitely
s4.h3_4_p1: Hesitation can be healthy. It becomes a problem when it lasts for years and prevents you from living.
s4.tip: Making the "right" decision doesn't mean making the easiest decision, or the one that causes the least pain in the short term. It means making the decision that allows you and your loved ones to build something better in the long run.

s5.title: Divorce: what it practically involves
s5.p1: Before committing to it, it's useful to know what you're dealing with. Divorce can take several forms, and the process varies depending on your situation and country.
s5.p2: Uncontested divorce is the simplest and fastest when both parties agree on everything (child custody, property division, support payments). In many jurisdictions, it can be handled without going to court.
s5.p3: Fault-based divorce still exists in some places, but it's less common and takes longer. It requires proving serious breaches of marital obligations.
s5.p4: No-fault divorce applies when the couple has been separated for a required period, often one to two years depending on the jurisdiction.
s5.p5: In most cases, having a lawyer is recommended or required. Timelines vary from a few months to several years depending on complexity.
s5.p6: Financially, several elements come into play: division of shared assets, spousal support (if a significant gap in living standards exists), and child support.
s5.p7: Regarding children, a family court judge decides on custody if the parents can't agree. Joint custody is now the most commonly chosen arrangement, unless circumstances require otherwise.
s5.tip: You can consult a family law attorney for a free or low-cost initial consultation. Many bar associations offer legal aid consultations. Check with your local courthouse or legal aid office.

s6.title: Divorcing with children: what you really need to know
s6.p1: This is often the most dreaded part. And the most misunderstood.
s6.p2: Children don't come out of a divorce unscathed, that's true. But they also don't come out unscathed from a childhood spent in a home of constant tension. Research on the subject is clear: what damages children isn't so much their parents' separation, but how it's handled and the quality of co-parenting that follows.
s6.p3: A divorce managed with mutual respect, clear age-appropriate communication with the children, and two parents who continue to engage in their role, that can go very well. Not perfectly, but well.
s6.p4: What's hard for them is being caught in the middle of the parental conflict. Hearing bad things about one parent from the other. Feeling they have to choose. That's what needs to be avoided, not the separation itself.
s6.tip: Family mediation services exist to help parents organize the separation in the children's best interest, without going through a judicial battle. It's often an underestimated option, but very useful when emotions are still running high.

s7.title: After divorce: do you recover?
s7.p1: The short answer is yes. The honest answer is: yes, but not right away, and not without going through something.
s7.p2: The first weeks and months after a separation are often difficult, even when you're the one who chose to leave. Grieving a relationship, a shared life, a version of yourself, it takes time. That's not a sign it was a mistake.
s7.p3: Most people who have gone through a divorce say, with hindsight, that they found something essential: themselves. Their freedom to decide. Their energy. Sometimes even their joy.
s7.p4: That doesn't mean it's easy. It means it's possible.

s8.title: Is this test reliable?
s8.p1: This test is not a medical or legal diagnostic tool. It does not replace the advice of a therapist, lawyer, or doctor. It's designed to help you take stock of your situation in a structured way, not to tell you what to do.
s8.p2: Your answers are anonymous and are not recorded. No one else will see your results.

faq.q: When should you really consider divorce?
faq.a: When communication has been broken for a long time, when repair attempts haven't changed anything, when your health is suffering, or when there is violence in any form.

faq.q: Can you divorce with children without hurting them?
faq.a: What hurts children isn't so much the separation but how it's handled. A divorce managed with mutual respect and quality co-parenting can go very well.

faq.q: Do you recover from a divorce?
faq.a: Yes, but not right away. Most people who've been through a divorce say they found something essential: themselves, their freedom to decide, their energy.

quiz.introP1: Nobody asks this question lightly. If you're here, it's because something isn't right, or because you can no longer tell if things are still okay. Either way, that's already a lot to carry.
quiz.introP2: This test won't decide for you. No test can, and it would be dishonest to claim otherwise. But it can help you put words to what you're feeling, see things more clearly, and sometimes confirm what you already know deep down. Answer honestly, even when it's uncomfortable. That's where it becomes useful.
